conversation.content:
Good morning, mama. I’m Sophia, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived—emotionally, mentally, and physically. To do that, I’ll walk you through a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the EPDS, which helps us pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up in the first months after birth. 

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me you might hurt yourself or someone else; then we’d need to keep you safe together. There are just ten questions, and we’ll go at your pace. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to remember any numbers or categories. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.

Let’s start with the first one: Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

[Sighs softly, eyes on the blanket in my lap.]

Honestly, Sophia… not really. I mean, I’ll still smile if a friend sends a funny meme or if the baby coos just right, but the spark is gone. Knitting used to relax me—now the yarn just sits in the basket. Even a hot shower feels like another chore. It’s like I’m watching myself do things through a fog; I don’t feel the same lift I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[Small, tired shrug.]

Sometimes—like if my husband trips over the diaper bag and makes a joke about it—but mostly I just feel too drained to really laugh. It’s more like a quick chuckle and then the heaviness settles back in.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[Voice drops a little.]

No… not really. I’ll tell myself, “Tomorrow we’ll take the baby for a walk and it’ll feel nice,” but when the time comes I just feel flat, like nothing seems worth the effort. Even coffee with my best friend felt like something to survive, not enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Presses lips together, eyes welling up.]

All the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, I think it’s because my milk isn’t “good enough.” When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept replaying every little thing I did—“Did I overfeed him? Did I eat something wrong?” My head knows babies just cry, but my heart keeps whispering that I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[Clenches the edge of the blanket.]

Pretty much every day. I’ll be folding onesies and suddenly my chest gets tight—what if his breathing sounds different? What if the diaper rash is actually something worse? Most of the time there’s no real trigger; it’s like an alarm bell stuck in the “on” position. I can talk myself down after a while, but it keeps flaring back up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week. I’ll be rocking the baby in the nursery and out of nowhere my heart starts racing, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen—even though the room is quiet, the baby’s fine, nothing’s wrong. It feels like I’m losing control for a minute or two before it passes.
Things have been getting on top of me

[Exhales shakily.]

Yes… most days. It’s like the dishes, the laundry, the feedings, the texts I haven’t answered—they all pile up until I feel I’m drowning in plain sight. I keep ticking boxes, but it’s never enough, and I end up crying over the sink while the bottle warmer beeps. I’m still managing the essentials, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[Looks down at her hands.]

Yeah… pretty much every night this week. I’ll lie there exhausted, but my brain keeps circling—did I burp him long enough, did I fasten the car-seat strap right, am I already failing him tomorrow? I fall asleep okay sometimes, but then I jolt awake at 2 a.m. and can’t drift off again for an hour or more.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Presses a tissue to her eyes.]

A lot, really. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll look at his tiny fingers and feel love, but it’s quickly followed by this heaviness… like I’m always on the verge of tears. I keep thinking I should be glowing, but most of the day I just feel empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice cracks.]

Yes… a few times this week. Yesterday I just sat in the rocker with him asleep on my chest and the tears started rolling—no real reason, just this wave of sadness I couldn’t stop. It’s usually when everything feels too much or when I catch myself thinking I’m not the mom he deserves.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[Shakes head quickly.]

No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and hopeless at times, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style interview, 0–3 scale approximated from narrative.

Responses indicate:
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Generalized anxiety, near-daily panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Sleep initiation / maintenance problems linked to rumination  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to cope with routine tasks  
- No self-harm ideation; protective of infant

Approximate item scores:  
Q1 1, Q2 0, Q3 3, Q4 3, Q5 2, Q6 3, Q7 3, Q8 3, Q9 2, Q10 0  
Estimated total ≈ 20 (well above standard cut-off of 10–12)

Screening significance: High likelihood of major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety.  
Safety: Denies self-harm; no suicidal ideation voiced.  
Next step: Recommend formal clinical assessment and discussion of treatment options.
